Long case 08 · General Surgery

Varicose Veins

The case with the widest gap between what you will be examined on and what is actually done. S Das teaches nine clinical tests; Bailey & Love 28e says in one sentence that the tourniquet tests have been abandoned. You need both, and you need to know which is which.

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1The case in one breath

Scale, and why the subject is neglected
Incidence is about 5% of the adult population.SRB 1 · p.222 B&L makes a point of the attitude problem: "Despite the considerable importance placed on lower limb function during the management of orthopaedic and arterial diseases, venous diseases are often forgotten or dismissed as cosmetic practice." And the counter-evidence: "Surgical intervention has been revolutionised by the development of endovenous techniques, and level 1 evidence has demonstrated that treatment can be associated with very high clinical- and cost-effectiveness."B&L 62 · p.1025 Open with that and you have already framed the case as a treatable disease rather than a cosmetic one.
Why the lower limb
SRB: "Varicosities are more common in lower limb because of erect posture and long column of blood has to be supported which can lead to weakness and incompetency of valves."SRB 1 · p.222
Definitions by calibre, which you will be asked
Dermal flares are thread veins under 1 mm in diameter, seen in 30% of superficial vein incompetence. Reticular veins are 1 to 3 mm, just deep to the skin, also in 30%. Varicose veins are usually over 3 mm.SRB 1 · p.222 Giving the millimetre thresholds separates a candidate who has read SRB from one who has not.
The two systems, in proportion
Superficial veins carry 10% of the venous system, lie in condensed superficial fascia between skin and deep fascia, have thick muscular walls, low pressure and plenty of valves. The long saphenous vein is the longest vein in the body and has 10 to 20 valves.SRB 1 · p.222
And what drives the circulation
B&L: venous pressure in the leg is increased by compression by the surrounding muscles, the calf muscle pump, and to a lesser extent by the tone of the venous wall. The deep calf veins are capacious and joined by blind-ending sacks, the soleal sinusoids, which force blood into the popliteal and crural veins during calf muscle pump contraction, for instance while walking.B&L 62 · p.1027 That is why exercise relieves venous symptoms and standing worsens them, and why compression works.
The four routes of superficial-to-deep communication SRB's list, and it is the anatomical skeleton of the whole examination: the saphenofemoral junction, mid-thigh perforators, the short saphenopopliteal junction, and calf perforators.SRB 1 · p.222 S Das's version for the long saphenous system, in order of importance: the saphenofemoral junction, which is the most important, the mid-thigh perforator, the lower-thigh perforator, and the lower leg perforators on the medial side.Das 7 · p.103

And the rule that makes a perforator "incompetent": perforators normally drain only from superficial to deep across a valve. In incompetence the flow reverses, from deep towards superficial, as "blow outs" which are more prominent during calf contraction.SRB 1 · p.222

2Why this patient has varicose veins

PrimarySecondary
Cause Often familial, cause unknown; weak valve or weak wall Acquired
AgeYoungerAdult and old
Veins affected Main saphenous veins; deep veins usually patent Saphenous, perforators and often deep veins
TestsOnly Trendelenburg test I positive Both Trendelenburg I and II often positive
ComplicationsLess, and lateCommon, and quick

SRB ch.1 p.222. Note that this classification is built on the Trendelenburg tests, which is exactly what the first conflict box below is about.

Primary causes, in full
Congenital incompetence or absence of valves; weakness or wasting of muscles with defective connective tissue and smooth muscle in the venous wall; stretching of the deep fascia; inheritance, with the FOXC2 gene; and the syndromes with varices of atypical distribution, Klippel-Trenaunay, avalvulia and Parkes-Weber.SRB 1 · p.222 The FOXC2 gene is the kind of specific that pays off in a viva.
Secondary causes, in full
Recurrent thrombophlebitis; occupational prolonged standing, SRB naming traffic police, guards and sportsmen; obstruction to venous return from abdominal tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis, lymphadenopathy or ascites; pregnancy, due to progesterone, plus obesity and chronic constipation; arteriovenous malformations; iliac vein thrombosis; and tricuspid incompetence.SRB 1 · p.222 The last is the one nobody expects and it is worth naming.
What B&L adds about mechanism
"The majority of patients with venous disease have a problem primarily with the vein wall structure and in most this is confined to the superficial veins. Little is known about the mechanism of initiation."B&L 62 · p.1027 So the honest answer to "what causes primary varicose veins?" is that it is a vein wall disease of largely unknown initiation, with a familial tendency. Being candid about that is better than reciting a list as though it were established causation.
And one named cause of obstruction worth knowing
May-Thurner syndrome, compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery, clearly described by May and Thurner in 1957.B&L 62 · p.1027 It is the reason a unilateral left-sided presentation with swelling deserves imaging of the pelvic veins.

3History, and why each question earns its place

What exactly troubles you: the appearance, the aching, or something else? WhyBecause the answer decides whether to treat at all, and because B&L's framing of the field is that venous disease is wrongly dismissed as cosmetic.B&L 62 · p.1025
SRB's symptom groupingGroup I, asymptomatic: venous telangiectasia, thread, reticular or varicose veins. Group II, symptomatic: cramps, heaviness, tenderness, itching, swelling. Group III, complicated: haemorrhage, superficial thrombophlebitis, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcers.SRB 1 · p.222
The classical symptomDragging pain and postural discomfort.SRB 1 · p.222
Is it worse in the morning or the evening? Rules inVenous. SRB: "Symptoms are less severe in morning than at evening."SRB 1 · p.222
WhyBecause the symptoms are from ambulatory venous hypertension, which accumulates through a day of standing and is relieved by a night of elevation. That diurnal pattern is what separates venous aching from arterial or musculoskeletal pain, and it is a single question.
ContrastArterial claudication is brought on by walking a predictable distance and relieved by standing still; venous aching is brought on by standing still and relieved by walking and elevation. If the patient says walking helps, think venous.
What is your occupation? How long do you stand? Rules inA secondary, occupational contribution. SRB names traffic police, guards and sportsmen, and lists prolonged standing and muscular weakness as contributory factors even in primary disease.SRB 1 · p.222 In Indian practice this is a very common and very relevant history.
Has anyone in your family had this? Rules inPrimary disease, which is often familial, with the FOXC2 gene implicated.SRB 1 · p.222
Have you ever had a swollen, painful leg, a clot, a long illness in bed, or a fracture? Rules inPost-thrombotic limb, that is secondary varicose veins with deep venous damage, and this is the single most important question in the history because it changes the treatment completely: you cannot strip or ablate a superficial vein that is the limb's collateral drainage.
Why it matters so muchSRB: 50% of venous ulcers are due to varicose veins and 50% are due to deep venous disease,SRB 1 · p.27 and "fifty percent of venous ulcer occurs as a result of recanalisation of DVT, and the leg is commonly called as postphlebitic limb".SRB 1 · p.234
SoHalf of the ulcers in this case are not primarily a superficial vein problem at all.
In a woman: how many pregnancies, and did the veins appear during one? Rules inPregnancy as a secondary cause, SRB attributing it to progesterone.SRB 1 · p.222 And SRB notes varicose veins are common in females.SRB 1 · p.27
Practical consequenceVeins appearing in pregnancy often regress after delivery, so intervention is usually deferred.
Any bleeding from the veins? Any ulcer, and where? Rules inComplicated, SRB's group III: haemorrhage, superficial thrombophlebitis, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis, venous ulcer.SRB 1 · p.222 Complications are an indication for intervention, not just for compression.
Where the ulcer should beSRB locates it precisely: around the ankle, in the gaiter's zone, from ambulatory chronic venous hypertension.SRB 1 · p.27 An ulcer elsewhere on the leg is probably not venous.
And the mechanism of the post-thrombotic ulcerDeep vein thrombosis causes increased venous pressure around the ankle transmitted through the perforators.SRB 1 · p.27

4Examination, and what each finding settles

Are the tourniquet tests still worth doing? S Das 7 p.102–104 teaches nine tests and SRB 1 p.222 classifies by them; B&L 62 p.1031 says they "have now been abandoned"
S Das
Devotes three pages to the clinical tests, and treats them as decisive: of the Brodie-Trendelenburg test he says "the positive tests are indications for operation".Das 7 · p.102 The battery is the Brodie-Trendelenburg test in two forms, the tourniquet test at successive levels, Perthes' test and a modified Perthes' test, the Schwartz test, Pratt's test, a cough impulse test, and direct palpation for fascial gaps at marked sites of perforators.Das 7 · p.102–104
SRB
Builds its entire primary-versus-secondary classification on them: in primary disease "only Trendelenburg test-I is positive", in secondary "both Trendelenburg tests I and II are often positive".SRB 1 · p.222 It also describes the Brodie-Trendelenburg test in detail.SRB 1 · p.223
Bailey & Love 28e
One sentence, under the heading Investigation: "Tourniquet tests and the use of hand-held Doppler have now been abandoned. There is good evidence to support the policy of duplex ultrasound scanning for all patients with varicose veins prior to any intervention."B&L 62 · p.1031 And the eponymous tests have gone with them: Perthes, Schwartz, Pratt, Fegan and Morrissey do not appear anywhere in chapter 62, and the only mention of Trendelenburg is the position on the operating couch and the eponym footnote.B&L 62 · p.1033
This is the widest gap between examination and practice in the whole of the long cases, and the answer is to do both and say why.

In the clinical examination, perform the tests. Your examiner is marking from S Das and SRB, the tests cost nothing, and performing them competently demonstrates that you understand superficial-to-deep reflux. Do the Brodie-Trendelenburg test properly, in both of its parts, and localise perforators with the tourniquet at successive levels.

Then say the sentence that shows you know where they stand: "These tests localise reflux clinically, but Bailey and Love 28e regards tourniquet tests and hand-held Doppler as abandoned, and the current standard is duplex ultrasound for every patient before any intervention, because treatment is now planned on the individual's mapped anatomy."B&L 62 · p.1031

Why they were abandoned, which is the real content: B&L explains that "the best clinical results come from clinicians who are personally very skilled in the use of duplex ultrasound and use it to design a bespoke treatment for each individual patient, based upon their unique anatomy".B&L 62 · p.1031 The tests give a yes or no at a crude level; duplex gives a map. Since modern treatment is catheter-directed into a named vein, a map is what you need. The tests were not shown to be wrong, they were made insufficient.

Do not, in an Indian examination, decline to perform the tests on the grounds that B&L has abandoned them. Perform them, then locate them.

Inspection, standing

Expose both legs fully and examine standing
Varices only fill against gravity. Mark the varicosities: SRB illustrates that veins should be marked just prior to surgery using marking ink.SRB 1 · p.228
Which system
Long saphenous: medial side of leg and thigh, anterior to the medial malleolus. Short saphenous: posterior calf, from the lateral side of the dorsal venous arch, passing posterior to the lateral malleolus with the sural nerve.B&L 62 · p.1026 The nerve matters because it is what gets injured.
The skin changes, in the order they develop
Pigmentation, that is haemosiderosis, then eczema, then lipodermatosclerosis of the calf skin, then ulceration.B&L 62 · p.1029 SRB adds atrophie blanche: white patches in the skin due to severe varicose veins.SRB 1 · p.222 S Das's instruction: look for pitting oedema or thickening, redness or tenderness at the lower part of the leg; these changes are due to chronic venous hypertension following deep vein thrombosis.Das 7 · p.104
Saphena varix, and the trap
SRB: a large varicosity in the groin which becomes visible on standing, with a positive cough impulse at the saphenofemoral junction.SRB 1 · p.223 B&L's warning: it "may elicit an impulse and it may be mistaken for a groin hernia".B&L 62 · p.1031 It is the same trap that appears in the hernia case from the other direction.
And the bone change nobody looks for
SRB: thickening of the tibia occurs due to periostitis in long-standing disease.SRB 1 · p.223

The tests, performed properly

Brodie-Trendelenburg test, both parts. SetupPatient recumbent, legs raised to empty the veins, hastened by milking the veins proximally. Compress the saphenofemoral junction with the thumb, or apply a tourniquet just below it, and ask the patient to stand up quickly.Das 7 · p.102
Part 1, release the pressureIf the varices fill very quickly by a column of blood from above, the saphenofemoral valve is incompetent. Positive Trendelenburg test.
Part 2, maintain the pressure for about a minuteGradual filling of the veins while the junction stays occluded indicates incompetent communicating veins, mostly on the medial side of the lower half of the leg, allowing flow from deep to superficial.Das 7 · p.102
SoPart 1 tests the junction; part 2 tests the perforators. Saying which part tests what is the whole point, and it is why SRB can use test I and test II to separate primary from secondary disease.SRB 1 · p.222
For the short saphenous systemThe same test, pressing the saphenopopliteal junction.Das 7 · p.102
Tourniquet test at successive levels. LogicA variant of the Trendelenburg test. Empty the veins by elevation, tie the tourniquet at a chosen level, stand the patient up. If the veins above the tourniquet fill and those below stay collapsed, the incompetent perforator is above the tourniquet. If those below fill rapidly while those above stay empty, it is below. Move the tourniquet down in steps and you localise it.Das 7 · p.102–103
One paradox S Das flagsIn short saphenous incompetence, a tourniquet on the upper thigh paradoxically increases the strength of the reflux, with faster filling, because it blocks the long saphenous route that was carrying most of the superficial return and throws the saphenopopliteal leak into prominence. S Das calls this pathognomonic of short saphenous varices.Das 7 · p.103 That is an unusual and memorable point.
And the definitive short saphenous testMark the saphenopopliteal junction with the patient standing; empty the vein by elevation; apply firm thumb pressure to the ink mark; stand the patient; release. Immediate filling confirms saphenopopliteal incompetence.Das 7 · p.103
Perthes' test: which one? S Das gives two different tests under one name S Das 7 p.103 describes the original and a "modified" version that work in opposite directions
Perthes' test, as S Das first gives it
"The affected lower extremity is wrapped with elastic bandage. With the elastic bandage on the patient is instructed to move around and exercise. Severe crampy pain is complained of if there is deep vein thrombosis. Of course arterial occlusive disease should be excluded."Das 7 · p.103 So the end point is pain.
Perthes' test, modified, on the same page
"This test is primarily intended to know whether the deep veins are normal or not. A tourniquet is tied round the upper part of the thigh tight enough to prevent any reflux down the vein. The patient is asked to walk quickly with the tourniquet in place. If the communicating and the deep veins are normal the varicose veins will shrink whereas if they are blocked the varicose veins will be more distended."Das 7 · p.103 So the end point is the size of the varices.
Bailey & Love 28e
Carries neither: the name Perthes does not appear in chapter 62 at all, and tourniquet tests as a class are described as abandoned.B&L 62 · p.1031
Both versions ask the same question, "are the deep veins patent?", by opposite signs, so answer by naming the question first and the method second.

Say: "Perthes' test assesses deep venous patency. The limb is bandaged or a thigh tourniquet applied to occlude the superficial system, and the patient is exercised. If the deep veins are patent the varices empty and the patient is comfortable; if the deep veins are obstructed the superficial veins become more distended and the patient develops severe crampy pain, because you have occluded the only drainage the limb has."Das 7 · p.103 That single sentence contains both versions and the mechanism, so you cannot be caught whichever one the examiner has in mind.

And say why it matters, because this is the test whose purpose survives even though the method has been superseded: if the deep veins are obstructed, the superficial veins are the limb's collateral drainage and must not be stripped or ablated. The modern way to answer that question is duplex, which B&L lists as one of the explicit aims of the scan: "the presence of obstruction in the deep venous system".B&L 62 · p.1031 Exclude arterial occlusive disease before interpreting exercise-induced pain, as S Das instructs.Das 7 · p.103
Schwartz test
In a long-standing case, a tap on the long saphenous varicosity in the lower leg transmits an impulse felt at the saphenous opening by the other hand. The percussion wave can also be transmitted from above downwards.Das 7 · p.103, p.104 It demonstrates a continuous column of blood in an incompetent vein.
Pratt's test, for leg perforators
Apply an Esmarch elastic bandage from toes to groin, then a tourniquet at the groin, which empties the varices. Keep the tourniquet, remove the bandage, then reapply the bandage from the groin downwards. At the site of each perforator a "blow out" or visible varix appears, and these are marked with a skin pencil.Das 7 · p.103–104
Cough impulse test
Elevate the limb to empty the veins, lay the patient down and ask for a forcible cough. An expansile impulse is felt in the long saphenous vein, particularly at the saphenous opening, if the saphenofemoral valve is incompetent; a bruit may be heard on auscultation.Das 7 · p.104
Palpating for the perforators directly
Mark the sites of excessive bulges while the patient stands. Lie him down, elevate the limb to empty the veins, and palpate along the marked line for gaps or pits in the deep fascia which transmit the incompetent perforators.Das 7 · p.104 This is the one test that is pure palpation and it is often the most convincing at the bedside.
Do not forget the rest of the leg, or the abdomen Examine the arterial system, because S Das makes excluding arterial occlusive disease a precondition for interpreting Perthes' test,Das 7 · p.103 and because compression is dangerous in an ischaemic limb. Examine the abdomen and pelvis, because SRB's secondary causes include abdominal tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis, lymphadenopathy and ascites.SRB 1 · p.222 And in a young patient with unilateral atypical varices and a limb length or girth difference, think of Klippel-Trenaunay.SRB 1 · p.222B&L 62 · p.1047

5Investigations

One investigation, and it is not optional Duplex ultrasound for every patient with varicose veins before any intervention.B&L 62 · p.1031 If you remember one sentence of management from this case, remember that one.
What the duplex scan must answer
B&L lists the aims explicitly: the presence of reflux in the deep and superficial venous system; the exact distribution and extent of reflux in the superficial system, including affected junctions and perforators; the presence of obstruction in the deep venous system; and the suitability of the vein for the planned intervention.B&L 62 · p.1031 Those four map precisely onto what the clinical tests were trying to do, which is why duplex replaced them.
The technical detail, if asked
A high-frequency linear array transducer of 7.5 to 13 MHz suits most lower limbs. B-mode settings are optimised so that the lumen appears as a dark void, and the Doppler settings for the low flow velocities encountered in veins. Visible venous flow can be augmented by a calf squeeze.B&L 62 · p.1031
An anatomical trap the scan exists to avoid
B&L: the anterior accessory great saphenous vein is commonly mistaken for the great saphenous vein itself, and a true duplex great saphenous vein is rare.B&L 62 · p.1026 SRB's equivalent surgical warning: a double saphenous vein is the most common anomaly near the saphenovenous junction.SRB 1 · p.228 Treating the wrong vein is a classic cause of recurrence.
The classification to quote
CEAP: Clinical, aEtiology, Anatomy, Pathophysiology, widely utilised,B&L 62 · p.1029 and updated in 2020.B&L 62 · p.1050 SRB gives its own group I, II and III symptom classification and then says "CEAP classification is also important",SRB 1 · p.222 so both books want you to know it. Give CEAP by name and expand the acronym; most candidates cannot.
And the other tests, in their place
SRB's broader workup for vascular lesions includes Doppler study, radiographs of the part, ECG and echocardiography.SRB 1 · p.211 Imaging of the pelvic and iliac veins is indicated when obstruction is suspected, for instance in May-Thurner syndrome.B&L 62 · p.1027

6Treatment, and the reasoning behind each choice

Is ligation and stripping still the operation? SRB 1 p.228 teaches Trendelenburg operation with stripping; B&L 62 p.1033 says endothermal ablation replaced it as the gold standard
SRB
Teaches the open operation in detail. Trendelenburg operation, or crossectomy, is juxtafemoral flush ligation of the long saphenous vein, flush with the femoral vein, after ligating the named tributaries, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal and superficial epigastric, plus the deep external pudendal and the unnamed tributaries. "All tributaries should be ligated, otherwise recurrence will occur."SRB 1 · p.228 And for a venous ulcer, the specific treatment is "Trendelenburg operation, stripping of veins, perforator ligation".SRB 1 · p.234
Bailey & Love 28e
"Endothermal ablation technologies replaced surgical ligation and stripping as the gold standard treatment once randomised trials demonstrated that they were marginally safer, have extremely high technical efficacy, offer superior quality of life post procedure (with a rapid recovery) and equivalent improvements in quality of life in the longer term. The techniques are cost-effective as they can be performed as an outpatient under local anaesthetic."B&L 62 · p.1033 Its description of open surgery is framed as the traditional alternative, used "unless by patient choice", whose principles are "to fully dissect the point of junctional incompetence and to remove the refluxing axial vein and dilated tributaries".B&L 62 · p.1033, p.1037
Live and decisive, and the honest answer is that B&L describes current best practice while SRB describes the operation you will see and may assist at in most Indian hospitals. Give both, in that order, and name the reason for each.

Answer: "The current gold standard is endothermal ablation, laser or radiofrequency, done as an outpatient under local anaesthetic, because randomised trials showed it to be marginally safer, highly effective technically, with better quality of life and faster recovery, and cost-effective. Where endovenous facilities are not available, or by patient choice, open surgery remains effective: a Trendelenburg operation, that is juxtafemoral flush ligation of the long saphenous vein with ligation of all tributaries, because leaving a tributary causes recurrence, with stripping of the refluxing axial vein and ligation of incompetent perforators."B&L 62 · p.1033SRB 1 · p.228

Two points that make the answer stronger. First, the principle is the same in both operations: abolish the point of junctional incompetence and deal with the refluxing axial vein. The difference is whether you do it with a catheter or a knife. Second, whichever you do, duplex first, because the treatment is designed around the individual's mapped anatomy.B&L 62 · p.1031

The modern treatment ladder

Compression, and the warning that goes with it
Graduated compression hosiery is the conservative mainstay. But B&L is blunt about the hazard: "misapplication of compression hosiery can have serious consequences (pressure necrosis, tourniquet effects); thus assessment, prescription and application of compression hosiery" should be done properly.B&L 62 · p.1033 And exclude arterial disease before compressing a leg.
SRB's bandages, for the ulcerCharing Cross elastic multilayered compression bandage, once a week; low compression bandaging; graduated elastic compression stockings with a leak-proof absorbent dressing beneath; Unna boots; crepe bandage or stockings.SRB 1 · p.234
Endothermal ablation: how it works
Two technologies: laser ablation and radiofrequency ablation. Endovenous laser ablation uses a small flexible glass fibre inserted into the vein; laser energy, typically at 1470 nm, travels down the fibre and is absorbed at its tip, generating vigorous thermal energy.B&L 62 · p.1033
The set-up, which is examinableVaricosities are marked beforehand if concomitant phlebectomy or foam sclerotherapy is planned. The patient is positioned in the reverse Trendelenburg position; for the great saphenous vein, supine with the hip of the treated leg externally rotated.B&L 62 · p.1033 The vein is surrounded by tumescent local anaesthetic solution, which compresses the vein onto the treatment device and protects the surrounding tissue.B&L 62 · p.1033
Note the ironyThe one surviving use of Trendelenburg's name in B&L's venous chapter is the position on the table for the procedure that replaced his operation.B&L 62 · p.1033
Non-thermal, non-tumescent ablation
B&L notes the trade-off: the mechanical devices can make the procedure uncomfortable and "the device can 'snag' on the vein, tearing it or rarely stripping it altogether"; comparative studies suggest similar early efficacy but increased medium- and long-term recanalisation rates, and although the axial ablation is less painful, that advantage is lost when it is combined with phlebectomy.B&L 62 · p.1036
Foam sclerotherapy
Used alongside ablation for residual varicosities, and B&L notes a specific advantage: it allows direct and targeted delivery of adjuvant foam, for example to ablate areas of neovascularisation.B&L 62 · p.1035
Open surgery, when it is done
Usually under general anaesthesia, though some use locoregional, with infiltration of tumescent local anaesthesia around the vein. The principles: fully dissect the point of junctional incompetence and remove the refluxing axial vein and dilated tributaries.B&L 62 · p.1037 SRB's operative detail, and the reason for it: all tributaries at the saphenofemoral junction must be ligated or recurrence will occur, and a double saphenous vein is the commonest anomaly near the junction.SRB 1 · p.228
The venous ulcer
Healthy granulation tissue needs skin grafting, with a definitive procedure for the varicose veins after evaluation,SRB 1 · p.18 or a pinch graft.SRB 1 · p.234 And the sequencing matters: treat the venous hypertension, or the graft fails.
And one group to treat conservatively almost always Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome. B&L: "Virtually all patients with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome should be treated conservatively with compression hosiery", though some benefit from laser ablation of the naevus, stapling of the bones to avoid leg length discrepancy and occasional removal of large superficial varicose veins.B&L 62 · p.1047 The reason is that the superficial veins may be the limb's main drainage, which is the same principle as the post-thrombotic limb.

7Complications, and the deep vein thrombosis you must not miss

Superficial thrombophlebitis
In SRB's complicated group III, along with haemorrhage, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and ulceration.SRB 1 · p.222
Haemorrhage
From a varix eroding the skin. Treated by elevation and direct pressure, not by a tourniquet, and then definitively.
Deep vein thrombosis, and the signs S Das teaches
Homan's sign: passive forceful dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee extended stretches the calf muscles and produces pain.Das 7 · p.106 Moses' sign: calf tenderness elicited directly, by squeezing the calf muscles from side to side.Das 7 · p.106 So there are two ways of eliciting calf tenderness, indirect and direct, and knowing both names is worth a mark.
And the extreme form
S Das: with venous obstruction the limb swells and becomes oedematous, and when it becomes congested and blue this is phlegmasia cerulea dolens.Das 7 · p.106
The question that follows a tourniquet
SRB describes the manoeuvre and the danger together: after applying a tourniquet at the saphenofemoral junction the patient is made to walk and, without removing the tourniquet, the limb is examined, with the warning of chest pain, breathlessness and haemoptysis, that is pulmonary embolism.SRB 1 · p.217 Any discussion of deep venous disease should end with embolism.

8Rapid-fire viva

Describe the Brodie-Trendelenburg test.

With the patient recumbent, raise the leg to empty the veins, milking them proximally. Compress the saphenofemoral junction with the thumb or apply a tourniquet just below it, and stand the patient up quickly. Part one: release the pressure, and if the varices fill rapidly from above the saphenofemoral valve is incompetent. Part two: maintain the pressure for about a minute, and gradual filling means incompetent communicating veins allowing deep-to-superficial flow, mostly on the medial side of the lower leg.Das 7 · p.102 For the short saphenous system, press the saphenopopliteal junction instead. Part one tests the junction; part two tests the perforators.

Are these tests still used?

In the clinical examination, yes, and I would perform them. But Bailey and Love 28e states that tourniquet tests and hand-held Doppler have now been abandoned, and that there is good evidence for duplex ultrasound in all patients with varicose veins before any intervention, because the best results come from clinicians who use duplex to design a bespoke treatment based on the patient's unique anatomy.B&L 62 · p.1031 The tests give a crude yes or no; duplex gives a map, and modern catheter-based treatment needs a map. Perthes, Schwartz, Pratt, Fegan and Morrissey do not appear in chapter 62 at all.

How do you distinguish primary from secondary varicose veins?

Primary: often familial, cause unknown, a weak valve or wall, younger patient, main saphenous veins affected, deep veins usually patent, only Trendelenburg test I positive, complications fewer and later. Secondary: acquired, adult or elderly, saphenous veins, perforators and often the deep veins involved, both Trendelenburg tests I and II often positive, complications common and quick to develop.SRB 1 · p.222 The crucial history is a previous deep vein thrombosis, immobility or fracture, because in a post-thrombotic limb the superficial veins are the collateral drainage and must not be removed.

What is Perthes' test for?

Deep venous patency. The superficial system is occluded, either by an elastic bandage or by a thigh tourniquet, and the patient exercises. If the deep veins are patent the varices shrink and the patient is comfortable; if they are obstructed the varices become more distended and the patient gets severe crampy pain, because you have occluded the limb's only drainage. S Das describes both versions, one judged by pain and the "modified" one by the size of the varices.Das 7 · p.103 Exclude arterial occlusive disease first. The modern equivalent is one of the stated aims of the duplex scan: the presence of obstruction in the deep venous system.B&L 62 · p.1031

Name the sites of superficial-to-deep communication.

The saphenofemoral junction, which is the most important; mid-thigh perforators; the short saphenopopliteal junction; and the calf perforators on the medial side.SRB 1 · p.222Das 7 · p.103 Normally perforators drain only superficial to deep across a valve; in incompetence the flow reverses as "blow outs", more prominent during calf contraction.SRB 1 · p.222

What is Pratt's test?

A test for the sites of leg perforators. An Esmarch elastic bandage is applied from toes to groin and a tourniquet tied at the groin, emptying the varices. Keeping the tourniquet, the bandage is removed and then reapplied from the groin downwards; at each perforator a blow-out or visible varix appears, and these are marked with a skin pencil.Das 7 · p.103

What is the Schwartz test?

A tap on the long saphenous varicosity in the lower leg transmits an impulse that can be felt at the saphenous opening with the other hand, demonstrating a continuous column of blood in an incompetent vein; the wave can also be transmitted from above downwards.Das 7 · p.103, p.104

What investigation would you order, and what must it tell you?

Duplex ultrasound, in every patient, before any intervention. It must establish: reflux in the deep and superficial systems; the exact distribution and extent of superficial reflux, including which junctions and perforators are affected; obstruction in the deep system; and the suitability of the vein for the planned intervention.B&L 62 · p.1031 A 7.5 to 13 MHz high-frequency linear array transducer suits most limbs, and flow can be augmented by a calf squeeze.

What is CEAP?

Clinical, aEtiology, Anatomy, Pathophysiology: the descriptive classification for chronic venous disorders, widely used and updated in 2020.B&L 62 · p.1029, p.1050 SRB gives its own symptom grouping, asymptomatic group I, symptomatic group II with cramps, heaviness, tenderness, itching and swelling, and complicated group III with haemorrhage, superficial thrombophlebitis, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and venous ulcer, and adds that CEAP is also important.SRB 1 · p.222

What is the gold standard treatment?

Endothermal ablation, laser or radiofrequency, which replaced ligation and stripping once randomised trials showed it to be marginally safer, technically highly effective, with superior quality of life and rapid recovery, equivalent long-term quality of life, and cost-effective because it is done as an outpatient under local anaesthetic.B&L 62 · p.1033 Open surgery remains appropriate where endovenous facilities are unavailable or by patient choice, and the principle is identical: abolish the point of junctional incompetence and deal with the refluxing axial vein.

Describe the Trendelenburg operation.

Juxtafemoral flush ligation of the long saphenous vein, flush with the femoral vein, after ligating the named tributaries, superficial circumflex iliac, superficial external pudendal and superficial epigastric, plus the deep external pudendal and the unnamed tributaries. All tributaries must be ligated or recurrence will occur. It is also called crossectomy, and is usually combined with stripping of the vein and ligation of incompetent perforators.SRB 1 · p.228, p.234 The commonest anomaly near the junction is a double saphenous vein, which is a cause of recurrence if missed.

How does endovenous laser ablation work?

A small flexible glass fibre is passed into the vein and laser energy, typically at 1470 nm, is transmitted down it and absorbed at the tip, generating vigorous thermal energy that ablates the vein. The vein is surrounded by tumescent local anaesthetic, which compresses it onto the device and protects surrounding tissue, and the patient is positioned in reverse Trendelenburg.B&L 62 · p.1033 Varicosities are marked beforehand if phlebectomy or foam sclerotherapy is to be done at the same time.

Where is a venous ulcer, and why there?

Around the ankle, in the gaiter's zone, due to ambulatory chronic venous hypertension, from long or short saphenous or perforator incompetence, or from a post-phlebitic limb.SRB 1 · p.27 Fifty per cent of venous ulcers are due to varicose veins and fifty per cent to deep venous disease, half of those from recanalisation after a deep vein thrombosis, giving the post-phlebitic limb.SRB 1 · p.27, p.234 In deep venous disease the pressure reaches the ankle through the perforators.

How would you treat a venous ulcer?

Compression is the mainstay: Charing Cross multilayered elastic compression once a week, graduated elastic stockings with a leak-proof absorbent dressing beneath, Unna boots, or low compression bandaging. Once there is healthy granulation tissue, skin grafting or a pinch graft. And a definitive procedure for the varicose veins after evaluation: Trendelenburg operation, stripping and perforator ligation.SRB 1 · p.18, p.234 Exclude arterial disease before compressing, and remember that misapplied compression hosiery can cause pressure necrosis and tourniquet effects.B&L 62 · p.1033

A lump in the groin with a cough impulse. Is it a hernia?

Not necessarily: a saphena varix is a large varicosity in the groin that becomes visible on standing and has a positive cough impulse at the saphenofemoral junction, and Bailey and Love warns it may be mistaken for a groin hernia.SRB 1 · p.223B&L 62 · p.1031 It is also the false positive that appears in the hernia case from the other direction. Duplex settles it.

Why do venous symptoms get worse through the day and better on walking?

Because they are caused by ambulatory venous hypertension, which accumulates with standing and is relieved by elevation overnight; SRB notes symptoms are less severe in the morning than the evening.SRB 1 · p.222 Walking activates the calf muscle pump: the capacious deep calf veins and their blind-ending soleal sinusoids force blood into the popliteal and crural veins during calf contraction.B&L 62 · p.1027 That is also the mechanism compression therapy exploits, and the reason arterial claudication is the mirror image, brought on by walking and relieved by rest.

Give the calibre definitions.

Dermal flares or thread veins are under 1 mm, seen in 30% of superficial vein incompetence. Reticular veins are 1 to 3 mm, lying just deep to the skin, also in 30%. Varicose veins are usually over 3 mm.SRB 1 · p.222 Atrophie blanche is the white patches that appear in the skin in severe disease.

Homan's sign and Moses' sign?

Two ways of eliciting calf tenderness in suspected deep vein thrombosis. Homan's is indirect: passive forceful dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee extended stretches the calf muscles and produces pain. Moses' is direct: squeezing the calf muscles from side to side.Das 7 · p.106 If venous obstruction progresses so the limb becomes congested and blue, that is phlegmasia cerulea dolens.

Why might varices be unilateral and the leg swollen?

Consider obstruction to venous return rather than simple valvular incompetence: abdominal tumour, retroperitoneal fibrosis, lymphadenopathy, ascites or iliac vein thrombosis.SRB 1 · p.222 And on the left specifically, May-Thurner syndrome, compression of the left common iliac vein by the right common iliac artery, described by May and Thurner in 1957.B&L 62 · p.1027 So examine the abdomen and image the pelvic veins.

Would you operate on varicose veins in Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome?

Almost never. Virtually all patients should be treated conservatively with compression hosiery, although some benefit from laser ablation of the naevus, stapling of the bones to avoid leg length discrepancy, and occasional removal of large superficial varices.B&L 62 · p.1047 The principle is the same as in a post-thrombotic limb: the superficial veins may be the limb's main drainage.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page so they can be found in a different edition. Where the books disagree, both positions are given and the amber boxes say which to answer. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love the venous system is chapter 62; SRB's venous material is inside its long chapter 1, which also covers ulcers, swellings and arterial disease. This is the case with the widest gap between the examination and current practice: the tourniquet tests that both Indian texts teach, and that SRB uses to classify the disease, are described by the 28th edition as abandoned in favour of duplex ultrasound. The guidance here is to perform them and then say where they stand.
